Parker signed Executive Order No. 7-25, her One Philly Plan to End Street Homelessness, during her State of the City speech on 19 December 2025. Its Section 1 is operative rather than advisory: it directs the Office of Homeless Services, in coordination with other City agencies, to facilitate access and provide financial support to operate 1,000 new shelter beds, to be operational by 31 January 2026, with on-site wrap-around behavioural health services and work with the Philadelphia Housing Authority on permanent supportive housing supply. Expanding the shelter system by 1,000 beds and directing financial support to operate them is chair 2, expanding services by increasing public funding. It is not chair 3, which is maintaining today's programmes with no major new spending, and it is not chair 1: the order sets a numbered expansion against a deadline rather than a permanent dedicated funding stream or a guarantee of housing.

Parker's first act in office was Executive Order No. 1-24, signed 2 January 2024, declaring a public safety emergency. It is not only a planning document: Section 2.A orders the Police Commissioner to employ any lawful means necessary to abate the emergency and the Department to vigorously enforce existing law, and Section 2.B sets the objective of increasing the number of police officers conducting patrol operations and maximising deployment of the current force. The Department's 100-Day Report, prepared in response to that order, records the delivery: strategies to maximise deployment of current staffing, strategies for increasing the number of officers trained for community policing, and 129 new officers assigned from academy classes to foot beats by the end of June 2024. Adding officers and expanding police presence to deter and respond to crime is chair 4. It is not chair 3, which keeps police as the main responders and adds crisis teams alongside them; the order's named objective is more officers and more patrol.

Parker signed six of the seven ICE Out bills into law on 7 May 2026, codifying Philadelphia's sanctuary policy in ordinance rather than leaving it to a predecessor's executive order. One of them adds Chapter 21-3600 to The Philadelphia Code, Non-Intervention with Respect to Immigration Enforcement. Its architecture is the judicial-warrant test: it defines an administrative warrant to include detainer requests while expressly excluding a judicial warrant or court order, and it bars City agencies from disclosing citizenship or immigration status unless required to do so by a judicial warrant or subpoena. The package likewise bars city agencies, including police, from collaborating with federal civil immigration enforcement absent a judicial warrant. Complying only on a court order is chair 2. Chair 1 is excluded by the document itself, which preserves 8 U.S.C. 1373 and states that nothing in the Chapter requires or permits violations of federal law, so local employees are not prohibited outright from sharing status information. It goes further than chair 3, which only declines proactive assistance: Philadelphia refuses the administrative detainer itself.

Krasner's first charging policy as District Attorney, the Philadelphia DAO New Policies effective 15 February 2018, states its own purpose as an effort to end mass incarceration and bring balance back to sentencing. A prosecutor's instrument is an office policy rather than a numbered ordinance, so this is classed as his own words. It directs his assistants to decline certain charges outright, to charge retail theft at the summary level on the stated rationale that summary gradation greatly reduces pre-trial incarceration rates because no bail is required, and to approach diversion and re-entry with greater flexibility while avoiding convictions where appropriate. Shrinking the jailed population by not charging and by diverting, rather than by adding beds, is chair 2. Chair 1 is excluded because it turns on redirecting incarceration funding into community mental health, addiction and housing programmes, and a district attorney directs charging rather than that budget. Chairs 4 and 5 are excluded because nothing in the policy builds or prioritises capacity.

Krasner's 2018 charging policy directs his office not to charge possession of marijuana regardless of weight, and not to charge the paraphernalia or buying-from-a-person offences where the drug is marijuana, while possession with intent to distribute remains prosecutable. That is real evidence of direction and it is his own instrument, but it does not settle a chair. Chair 3 would have him removing criminal penalties for personal possession while keeping commercial sales illegal, which describes the effect of the policy; chair 4 would have him legalising and regulating a taxed market, which a district attorney cannot do and which declining to prosecute neither affirms nor rules out. A prosecutor operating inside a law he did not write can hold either position, and nothing in the policy says which, so the value is left blank.

Brooks announced the People's Tax Plan in March 2025 as Minority Leader, and its centrepiece is a new levy rather than an adjustment: a revised version of her own 2022 wealth tax, a 0.4 percent charge on stocks and bonds above the first 100,000 dollars of assets, predicted to raise 200 million dollars a year. In her own words the plan is meant to ensure billionaires and corporations pay their fair share in taxes. Two years earlier she set out what the money is for, saying she would vote against tax cuts because tax cuts lead to service cuts and naming the services she wanted funded instead. Raising taxes on wealthy people and large companies in order to fund more public services is chair 1. Chair 3 is excluded because a wholly new tax on financial assets is not a targeted adjustment to the existing system. Chairs 4 and 5 are excluded outright, since she opposed the wage and business tax cuts her colleagues passed. Chair 2 is the closer call and is excluded on the second half of its text: it funds existing services, while her stated purpose is expanded ones.

Brooks secured the first direct city funding for Planned Parenthood in Philadelphia and has said the city must do everything in its power locally, across the state and nationally to ensure abortion providers remain open and safe. That is a clear direction and a real act, but this ladder does not ask whether someone supports access; every rung on it turns on how late in a pregnancy abortion should remain lawful. Chairs 1, 2 and 3 all sit on the side she is plainly on, and nothing she has said distinguishes keeping abortion legal at every stage from a second-trimester or first-trimester limit. Choosing among them would be a guess, so the value is left blank.

O’Rourke jointly announced the People’s Tax Plan in March 2025 as Minority Whip, a package whose centrepiece is a new 0.4 percent wealth tax on stocks and bonds projected to raise 200 million dollars a year. That would name chair 1 if the plan were his own words, but it is not: the release is issued by the Minority Wing and the wealth tax is attributed in it to his colleague. His own quoted words address only the other half of the package, expanding the Wage Tax Refund so that all poor and working-class Philadelphians can claim it. That is relief for low earners, which is compatible with chairs 1, 2 and 3 alike and does not say whether he would raise taxes on the wealthy to pay for it. This topic is own-words only at the local level, so the package cannot be read as a record either, and the value is left blank.

Chair 1 here is a compound claim, equal marriage plus protection from discrimination in areas such as jobs and housing, and only its second clause is evidenced: nothing in her record found here states a position on the legal recognition of same-sex marriage itself, which is what every rung on this ladder turns on. Seating chair 1 on the anti-discrimination half alone would assert the marriage half she has not been shown to have stated, so the value is left blank.

Gauthier chairs the Committee on the Environment and introduced legislation to restore the Sustainable Business Tax Credit, which gives an eligible business up to 8,000 dollars a year against its business tax, saying it is time to bring back a credit that rewards businesses that do well by doing good. This ladder asks how much government should do to expand clean energy, and the credit is not an energy measure: it rewards a broad triple-bottom-line standard rather than funding generation, grid or efficiency. Chair 2 is the nearest rung and it calls for major subsidies, tax credits and public investment in clean energy; an 8,000 dollar credit against one business tax is neither major nor aimed at energy. Her direction is plain but no rung describes this instrument, so the value is left blank.
